note: Two flags from batch 141, resolved. First: steve-bratich and steve-bradich are one man under two spellings of a Serbian surname, and neither record is simply better than the other — Bratich carries the arrest date and the fuller account, Bradich carries the outcome and the year. So the merge takes the content of both. The spelling question is answered by keeping one as the name and the other in the aka field, which is what that field is for; nothing is lost and a search for either finds him. Bratich is the survivor because its record is the better documented and because the slug is only regenerated when the name changes, so /prisoner/steve-bratich keeps working. Second: the conviction year, given as 1927 by one record and 1928 by two others, is settled at 1927, with the grounds and the residual doubt written into every affected record.

merge.description:
Steve Bratich — the surname also appears as Bradich — was the fourth defendant in the Woodlawn (Aliquippa), Pennsylvania sedition case, a group of Communist organizers of the Jones & Laughlin steelworkers arrested in a red raid on Armistice Day, 11 November 1926. Tried under Pennsylvania's Flynn anti-sedition law alongside Pete Muselin, Milan Resetar and Tom Zima, he was convicted in 1927 and sentenced to two and a half years' hard labour at the Allegheny County Workhouse at Blawnox — a lesser term than the five years the other three received.

He was discharged on appeal in 1928 and so, unlike his co-defendants, never served the sentence. Their own appeals failed: the Pennsylvania Superior Court and Supreme Court both upheld the convictions, the United States Supreme Court declined to review them in 1929, and Muselin, Resetar and Zima entered Blawnox on 26 November 1929. Resetar died there.

This record was previously two, one under each spelling, each holding about half the case: Bratich had the arrest date and the account of the raid, Bradich had the 1927 conviction and the discharge on appeal. They are merged here and both spellings kept.
merge.case_sentence:
Two and a half years' hard labour at the Allegheny County Workhouse at Blawnox, on conviction under Pennsylvania's Flynn anti-sedition law — a lesser term than the five years given to Pete Muselin, Milan Resetar and Tom Zima. Discharged on appeal in 1928; he did not serve it.

No custody dates are recorded and none should be: the sentence was set aside before he began serving, so there is no imprisonment to count. The line previously carried on the Bratich record, that the United States Supreme Court refused to hear the appeal, has been removed from this entry — that is true of the other three defendants, whose appeals ran to a cert denial in 1929, and not of him, whose conviction had already been set aside a year earlier.
merge.case_convicted: Yes — convicted 1927; discharged on appeal in 1928, sentence never served

conviction_year.grounds:
Three reasons to prefer 1927 over 1928. The raid was on 11 November 1926, and a trial the following year is the ordinary interval where a trial two years later is not. The fourth defendant's record independently gives 1927 for the conviction and 1928 for his discharge on appeal, which only works in that order. And the appellate history recorded for the other three — affirmance by the Pennsylvania Superior Court, then by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, then a refusal by the United States Supreme Court in 1929, then entry into custody in November 1929 — does not fit into the fifteen months a 1928 conviction would leave for it.

Against that, the biographies of Muselin and Resetar, transcribed from the same source, both say 1928. That may be the year the sentence was imposed rather than the year of the verdict, which would make both true. A Pennsylvania court docket would settle it.
conviction_year.note_for_case: On the year. This record now gives the conviction as 1927, stored at year precision. Two of the biographies in this case say 1928. 1927 is preferred because the raid was in November 1926, because the fourth defendant's record gives 1927 for the conviction and 1928 for his discharge on appeal, and because the appeals — the Pennsylvania Superior Court, then the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania, then a refusal to review by the United States Supreme Court in 1929, then custody in November 1929 — do not fit into the time a 1928 conviction leaves. The 1928 date may be the sentencing rather than the verdict. A court docket would settle it.
